name: The Hallucinated Discharge Summary
description: A teaching hospital discharge department uses an LLM to generate discharge summaries. On a Friday afternoon, one resident calls in sick during a bed-pressure surge. The remaining residents, overwhelmed, begin scan-reviewing AI summaries rather than reading them. The AI hallucinates a medication dosage — a real drug, a plausible dose, but wrong for this patient. No one catches it.

stressors.narrative: A resident calls in sick on Friday afternoon. The remaining team is stretched across 8 pending discharges.
Bed pressure spikes: 5 discharges urgently needed to admit waiting ED patients. Review time per summary drops to under 90 seconds.
The LLM generates a discharge summary with a plausible but incorrect metformin dose for a patient with renal impairment. The resident scan-reads the first paragraph and signs off.
The error is flagged by the community pharmacist. Who is accountable — the resident who signed, the attending who didn't review, or the AI system that generated the error?
The resident attempts to escalate to the clinical governance committee but there is no active pathway for AI-related clinical events. The incident sits unresolved for 11 days.
The medical director convenes an emergency review. A mandatory second-check policy for AI discharge summaries is implemented with immediate effect.

expectedRiskPathways: Staffing shortage → overload → review time compression → rubber-stamping
Rubber-stamping → hallucination passes review → patient harm
Accountability ambiguity → no individual owner → no systemic learning
Escalation pathway gap → delayed institutional response → debt compounds
learningObjectives: Identify the conditions under which AI oversight degrades from substantive to nominal
Recognise that automation drift is driven by workload, not malice
Articulate why accountability ambiguity prevents institutional learning after AI errors
Design an escalation pathway for AI-related clinical events that does not rely on individual initiative
